Part I — Knowledge Base (English)
Bhaiya's Teachings — Knowledge Base (Session 78, English)
Chandravanshi Series: Mahabhisha, Ganga, Bhishma's Vow , Satyavati, and Vidura's Origin — Plus Teachings on Mukti and the Natur e of Cr eation

Sour ce: a fr esh-day Ashaeiynn live session, opening with the sangat gathering and casual banter , a teaching on why liberation (mukti) is a myth and why history r epeats itself, a formal opening prayer , and then a continuation of the Chandravanshi teaching series — this time r eaching further back in the lineage than pr evious installments, covering Mahabhisha's curse and rebirth, Ganga's sons, Bhishma's vow , Satyavati's origin, and the birth of Dhritarashtra, Pandu, and V idura. The session closes with an extended cosmological teaching on Prakriti (natur e) and Sanskriti (cultur e), and Adi Shakti. This session contains genuine live back-and-forth (audience Q&A on dosh fr om r outine pest contr ol, and live engagement thr oughout), so it is pr ocessed as a full 3-part document.
1. Session Opening
Per this teaching's live texture, the session opens informally while the sangat gathers, with Bhaiya checking in on timing and encouraging latecomers to eat before joining, before beginning.
2. Series Planning: What Comes After Chandravanshi

Per this teaching, Bhaiya shares that once the Chandravanshi series concludes, the next series will be Suryavanshi, followed by a discussion of the spiritual power present across many religious traditions, including Buddhism and Jainism, and how Bhagwan Ram is referenced across dif ferent faiths.
3. Teaching: Mukti (Liberation) Is a Myth

Per this teaching, no great bhakta or siddha in history ever asked God for mukti; even the most exalted devotees (Kaag Bhushundi ji and others held up as models of ananya/exclusive devotion) asked only for bhakti itself, never liberation. Per this teaching, even a soul that achieves a subtle, karma-free state will eventually be found by someone else who bows to it — and the moment they are bowed to, karmic obligation (having to bless or respond) restarts. Per this teaching, even devas are not truly "free" in this sense, so pursuing mukti as a goal is described as misguided.
4. Teaching: History Repeats Itself

Per this teaching, in every birth a soul tries to improve on its previous life but tends to repeat the same patterns regardless; per this teaching, rather than exhausting oneself trying to recall a past life, the wiser path is to fully commit — "100%" — to whatever role or duty one currently holds.
5. Opening Prayer

Per this teaching's live practice, a formal prayer to Hanuman ji Maharaj is of fered, invoking Bhaiya's own sankalp (resolve) and requesting shakti, bhakti, tattva, gyaan, and bodh (wisdom and awakening).
6. Picking Up the Chandravanshi Narrative

Per this teaching, this installment continues directly from a previous day's stopping point (recalled live by the sangat as "Y adu and Puru," the two sons from the earlier part of the lineage), using the traditional narrative frame of the story being told to King Janmejaya by Rishi Vyasa's lineage of disciples.
7. Mahabhisha's Story and Indra's Curse

Per this teaching, King Mahabhisha earned heavenly reward through righteous living. In heaven, the apsara Ganga's ornament and garment slipped as she approached; while other devas modestly looked away , Mahabhisha and Ganga kept gazing at each other . Indra, angered, cursed Mahabhisha to be reborn as a mortal, and cursed Ganga to be reborn as well, in order to break Mahabhisha's heart in human form.
8. Mahabhisha Reborn as Pratipa

Per this teaching, Mahabhisha is reborn as King Pratipa, a righteous ruler of the Chandravanshi line, who has two sons, Devapi (the elder , unable to rule due to physical infirmity , who renounces the kingdom rather than live under his younger brother) and Shantanu, who is anointed king of Hastinapur .
9. Pratipa Meets the Young Ganga

Per this teaching, in his own later life of renunciation, Pratipa meets a beautiful young woman seated on his right thigh (a position signaling a daughter , not a wife); she asks to marry his son Shantanu, and Pratipa promises this on her behalf.
10. Shantanu and Ganga's Marriage and Its Condition

Per this teaching, Ganga agrees to marry Shantanu only if he never questions her actions, whatever they may be; he agrees, and she proceeds to drown each of their first seven newborn sons in the river without explanation.
1 1. The Eighth Son and the Revelation of the Eight Vasus

Per this teaching, when Shantanu finally stops her from drowning their eighth son, Ganga reveals that all eight sons were the eight Vasus, cursed by Rishi Vashishtha (guru to the Ram lineage) to live mortal lives after one of them, Prabhasa, stole the rishi's beloved cow for his wife. Per this teaching, the other seven Vasus were innocent and were mercifully freed quickly through drowning; only Prabhasa, the guilty one, was required to live a full, dif ficult mortal life — this eighth son is Devavrata, later known as Bhishma.
12. Shantanu's Vow to Devavrata
Per this teaching, Shantanu vows to give this son everything — kingship, marriage, and every advantage — and Devavrata is sent to train under Parshuram, becoming an extraordinarily powerful warrior .
13. Shantanu's Love for Satyavati

Per this teaching, Shantanu later falls in love with Satyavati, a woman raised by a fisherman, and proposes marriage; she agrees only on the condition that her own future sons — not Devavrata — inherit the throne.
14. Satyavati's True Origin

Per this teaching, Satyavati's origin traces to King Uparichara (Uchaya): his seed, entrusted to a bird for delivery to his wife, fell into a lake and was swallowed by a fish who was herself a cursed apsara (cursed by Brahma to remain a fish until she bore a human child). The fish was caught and found to contain twins: a boy , given to the king and raised as King Matsya, and a girl, given to the fisherman, who grew up smelling of fish and was known as Matsyagandha.
15. Sage Parashar and the Birth of Ved Vyas

Per this teaching, sage Parashar , crossing the river on Matsyagandha's boat, was moved by her wish to be free of her fishy smell and low social standing; he granted her a boon removing the smell and enhancing her beauty in exchange for union. Their son, born darkcomplexioned on a river island, became known as Krishna Dvaipayana — later Ved Vyas. Per this teaching, Matsyagandha (now transformed, and thereafter known as Satyavati) left the infant with Parashar and continued on with her life.
16. Devavrata's Vow and the Name Bhishma

Per this teaching, to remove any obstacle to his father's marriage to Satyavati, Devavrata vows lifelong celibacy and permanently renounces his own claim to the throne — a vow so severe that the devas themselves praised him, giving him the name Bhishma ("one of the terrible vow"). Per this teaching, some textual traditions (including certain Bengali versions of the Mahabharata) add that this vow was made irreversible through further physical means, though this teaching notes this detail varies by text.
17. Shantanu and Satyavati's Sons

Per this teaching, Shantanu and Satyavati have two sons: Chitrangada, who dies in single combat against a gandharva of the same name, and Vichitravirya, who survives but is physically unable to father children.
18. Bhishma's Abduction of the Three Princesses of Kashi

Per this teaching, when Vichitravirya is not invited to the swayamvar of the three princesses of Kashi (Amba, Ambika, and Ambalika), Bhishma, angered at the slight to Hastinapur , forcibly abducts all three princesses for his brother's marriage, defeating every rival king present.
19. Amba's Story and Her Vow of Vengeance

Per this teaching, the eldest princess, Amba, reveals she already loves King Shalva and wishes to return to him; Bhishma releases her , but Shalva rejects her for having been "won" in another man's procession. Rejected everywhere — by kshatriya kings, and even by Parshuram (who fights Bhishma to an inconclusive standstill, since Bhishma cannot be defeated due to his boon of choosing his own time of death) — Amba finally receives a boon from Bhagwan Shiva that she will cause Bhishma's death, but only in a future life; she immolates herself and is reborn as Shikhandi, child of King Drupad.
20. Vichitravirya's Death Without Heirs
Per this teaching, Vichitravirya proves unable to father children and dies young (accounts vary on the cause), leaving the throne without an heir .
21. Satyavati's Request and Bhishma's Refusal
Per this teaching, Satyavati asks Bhishma to break his vow and father heirs himself to save the line; Bhishma firmly refuses, upholding his original vow .
22. Satyavati Summons Ved Vyas

Per this teaching, Satyavati instead summons her first son, Ved Vyas, and asks him to father children with Ambika and Ambalika through niyoga (a sanctioned practice for producing an heir when the husband cannot).
23. The Birth of Dhritarashtra and Pandu

Per this teaching, Ambika, frightened by Vyas's ascetic appearance, closes her eyes during their union, and her son, Dhritarashtra, is born blind. Ambalika turns pale with fear during her own union with Vyas, and her son, Pandu, is born physically frail and pale.
24. The Birth of Vidura

Per this teaching, dissatisfied that neither son is fully fit to rule, Satyavati asks for one more attempt; this time, Ambika — too afraid to face Vyas again — sends her maidservant in her place. The maid, approaching without fear , bears a son who is capable in every way — Vidura — but who cannot become king because his mother is a maidservant.
25. Vidura's True Identity as an Incarnation of Yamraj

Per this teaching, Vidura is in fact an incarnation of Yamraj (the god of death and dharma), the result of a curse: Rishi Mandavya, though innocent, was wrongly executed alongside actual thieves after being caught in their company; when he confronted Yamraj about the injustice, Yamraj explained it as karmic justice for the rishi's own childhood act of killing insects. Mandavya protested this judgment as disproportionate and cursed Yamraj to himself experience, firsthand, the pain of loss and injustice as a mortal — leading to Yamraj's birth as Vidura.
26. Why Vidura Always Understood and Honor ed Krishna
Per this teaching, because of this origin and the lesson learned from it, Vidura is described as someone who deeply understood divine justice and never disrespected Bhagwan Krishna.
27. Bhaiya Defers the Rest of the Story

Per this teaching's live practice, Bhaiya pauses the narrative here, explaining he doesn't want to continue too long and risk the sangat growing sleepy , and promises to continue the remaining story in a later session.
28. Live Q&A: Routine Pest Contr ol and Dosh

Per this teaching's live practice, in response to a sangat member's question about whether routine insect-killing (insecticide spray , mosquito-swatting) carries the same karmic weight as the childhood act that led to Rishi Mandavya's curse, Bhaiya indicates the fuller context will become clear once the complete story is heard, without giving a final definitive answer in this exchange.
29. Extended Teaching: Why Mukti Is a Myth (Expanded)

Per this teaching, expanding on the earlier point, even a liberated being existing in a remote, empty universe will eventually be found by another traveler (Bhaiya humorously includes himself, as a practitioner of divya drishti, among such "wanderers" who visit many realms); the moment of being found and bowed to restarts the cycle of karmic obligation — introducing oneself, receiving and returning blessings — making full "escape" through liberation ef fectively impossible, and beside the point.
30. Teaching: Prakriti (Natur e) Cannot Be Altered Directly

Per this teaching, Prakriti (equated here with the entire cosmos, and ultimately with Adi Shakti, the primordial Mother) cannot itself be controlled or directly altered; to draw anything out of pure Prakriti, one must first establish a Sanskriti (a specific, bounded cultural/ener getic framework).
31. The Three Elements Needed to Establish a Sanskriti

Per this teaching, any such Sanskriti requires three elements: an Agni tattva (fire/creative-knowledge element, associated with Brahma), a Dev tattva (a specific awakened, rajasic deity), and a Shiv tattva (a completing, protective element) — together functioning as that culture's own Brahma, Vishnu, and Mahesh.
32. Countless Cultur es Within One Prakriti

Per this teaching, countless such "cultures," each with its own Brahma-V ishnu-Mahesh triad, exist within the single overarching Prakriti — which is why a specific deity within a specific culture can be challenged (as powerful aghori sadhaks are described as doing) and can be made to bow , whereas Prakriti itself (Adi Shakti) cannot be challenged by anyone.
33. The Origin of Adi Shakti

Per this teaching, Bhagwan Shiva's form as Sada Shiva meditates exclusively on Ram Tattva, which this teaching describes as the supreme (param) tattva, beyond Brahma, Vishnu, or Mahesh individually . Through this meditation, Shiva manifests the Shakti who sits beside him — Adi Shakti — meaning that, per this teaching's framing, Prakriti (Nature) itself ultimately originates from Ram Tattva by way of Shiva.
34. A Sangat Reflection on Pr ophecy

Per this teaching's live practice, a sangat member shares that they have separately been told about predictions involving the Kalki avatar and specific associated figures; Bhaiya declines to engage in prophecy himself, redirecting the focus back to studying one's own scriptures rather than speculating about the future.
35. Closing Teaching: The Value of Learning Scriptur e

Per this teaching, Bhaiya closes by ur ging the sangat to learn and remember these stories — not just from Hindu tradition but across all religious traditions — both for their own spiritual growth and to pass on to future generations; he notes that visiting sants engage meaningfully only with those who show genuine understanding, since wisdom, not blind devotion alone, is what makes a seeker able to receive and make use of deeper teachings.
36. Closing Blessing
Per this teaching, the session closes with a reminder to ask the divine chiefly for bhakti and the time to practice it, trusting that everything else follows — closing with "Jai Siyaram."
QUICK RULES SUMMARY

No great bhakta in this tradition has ever asked God for mukti (liberation) — only for bhakti itself; per this teaching, even a liberated soul is eventually found and bowed to by someone else, which restarts karmic obligation, so mukti is described as a myth not worth chasing. History repeats itself because each soul tends to repeat its own past patterns rather than fully escape them; the recommended focus is giving 100% to one's current role rather than chasing memory of past lives. Mahabhisha and the apsara Ganga were both cursed by Indra to take human birth after a breach of heavenly modesty; Mahabhisha was reborn as King Pratipa, whose son Shantanu later married the reborn Ganga. Ganga drowned her first seven sons with Shantanu (freeing the seven innocent Vasus from a curse); the eighth son, spared by Shantanu's intervention, was Devavrata (later Bhishma) — the one Vasu (Prabhasa) who bore actual guilt and had to live a full mortal life.

Devavrata vowed lifelong celibacy and renounced the throne so his father could marry Satyavati, earning the name Bhishma. Satyavati was the fish-born daughter of King Uparichara's seed and a cursed apsara; sage Parashar granted her beauty in exchange for union, and their son became Ved Vyas. After Vichitravirya (Shantanu and Satyavati's surviving son) died without heirs, Ved Vyas fathered Dhritarashtra (born blind, via Ambika's fear), Pandu (born frail, via Ambalika's fear), and Vidura (born to a maidservant, and thus unable to become king despite his full capability). Vidura is revealed as an incarnation of Yamraj, cursed by Rishi Mandavya after being wrongly executed for a minor childhood of fense (killing insects) — a curse condemning Yamraj to personally experience the pain of loss and injustice. A Prakriti (nature/cosmos) cannot be directly altered; drawing anything from it requires establishing a Sanskriti (culture) built from three elements — an Agni tattva, a Dev tattva, and a Shiv tattva — mirroring a local Brahma-V ishnu-Mahesh. Adi Shakti is Prakriti itself, before whom every culture's Brahma-V ishnu-Mahesh bows; she originates, per this teaching's framing, from Sada Shiva's meditation on the supreme Ram Tattva. Part II — Q&A Pairs (English)
Bhaiya's Teachings — Q&A Pairs (Session 78, English)
Chandravanshi Series: Mahabhisha, Ganga, Bhishma's Vow , Satyavati, and Vidura's Origin
User-style questions with answers gr ounded in this Ashaeiynn live session. Gr eeting style: "Jai Siyaram."

Q1. Does this teaching say a devotee should ask God for mukti (liberation)? A: No — per this teaching, no great bhakta in history ever asked for mukti; even the most exalted devotees asked only for bhakti (devotion) itself, since even a liberated soul is eventually found and bowed to by someone else, restarting karmic obligation.

Q2. Why does this teaching say true "fr eedom" fr om karmic bonds is effectively impossible? A: Per this teaching, because even a soul that reaches a subtle, karma-free state will eventually be encountered by another being who bows to it — and being bowed to itself creates an obligation to respond, restarting the cycle; per this teaching, even devas are not truly free in this sense.

Q3. Why does history r epeat itself, per this teaching? A: Per this teaching, because in every birth a soul tries to improve on its past life but tends to repeat the same underlying patterns; the recommended response is not to obsessively chase memory of a past life, but to commit fully to one's present role and duty .

Q4. Who was Mahabhisha, and why was he cursed? A: Per this teaching, Mahabhisha was a righteous king who earned a place in heaven; when the apsara Ganga's ornament and garment slipped, he kept gazing at her instead of looking away like the other devas, and Indra cursed both of them to take human birth as punishment.

Q5. Who did Mahabhisha become after being r eborn? A: Per this teaching, he was reborn as King Pratipa, whose younger son Shantanu later became king of Hastinapur (the elder son, Devapi, stepped aside due to physical infirmity).
Q6. Under what condition did Ganga agr ee to marry Shantanu? A: Per this teaching, she agreed only if Shantanu never questioned anything she did, however troubling it might appear .

Q7. What did Ganga do to their first seven sons, and why? A: Per this teaching, she drowned each of them in the river immediately after birth — later revealed to be a mercy , since all eight sons were the eight Vasus, cursed by Rishi Vashishtha to take mortal birth, and drowning quickly freed the seven who were innocent of the original of fense.

Q8. Who was the eighth son, and why was he tr eated differ ently? A: Per this teaching, the eighth son was Devavrata (later known as Bhishma) — the one Vasu (Prabhasa) who was actually guilty of stealing Rishi Vashishtha's cow , and who therefore had to live a full, dif ficult mortal life rather than being freed early .

Q9. Why is Devavrata called "Bhishma"? A: Per this teaching, because he took an extraordinarily severe ("bhishma") vow of lifelong celibacy and renounced his own claim to the throne, so that his father Shantanu could marry Satyavati — a vow so remarkable that the devas themselves praised him and gave him this name.
Q10. What was Satyavati's condition for marrying Shantanu? A: Per this teaching, that her own future sons, not Devavrata, would inherit the throne.

Q1 1. What is Satyavati's true origin story , per this teaching? A: Per this teaching, King Uparichara's seed, sent via a bird, fell into a lake and was swallowed by a cursed apsara living as a fish; when caught, the fish was found to contain twins — a boy raised as King Matsya, and a girl (Satyavati) raised by a fisherman, known early on as Matsyagandha for her fish-like smell.

Q12. How was Ved Vyas born, per this teaching? A: Per this teaching, sage Parashar , ferried across a river by Matsyagandha, granted her a boon removing her fish smell and enhancing her beauty in exchange for union; their son, born on a river island with a dark complexion, became Krishna Dvaipayana, later known as Ved Vyas.

Q13. What happened to Shantanu and Satyavati's two sons? A: Per this teaching, Chitrangada died in single combat against a gandharva of the same name, and Vichitravirya, though he survived, was physically unable to father children and died young without heirs.

Q14. Why did Bhishma abduct the thr ee princesses of Kashi? A: Per this teaching, because Vichitravirya was not invited to their swayamvar , an insult Bhishma would not tolerate; he defeated every rival king present and brought all three princesses back for his brother's marriage.

Q15. What happened to Amba, the eldest of the thr ee princesses? A: Per this teaching, she revealed she already loved King Shalva and was released by Bhishma, but Shalva rejected her; unable to find justice from any kshatriya king or even from Parshuram (who could not defeat Bhishma), she received a boon from Bhagwan Shiva that she would cause Bhishma's death in a future life, then immolated herself and was reborn as Shikhandi.

Q16. Why couldn't Bhishma be defeated even by Parshuram, per this teaching? A: Per this teaching, because Bhishma had a boon allowing him to choose his own time of death, making him ef fectively undefeatable in direct combat.

Q17. Why did Satyavati summon Ved Vyas after Vichitravirya's death? A: Per this teaching, because Bhishma refused to break his vow and father heirs himself, Satyavati turned to her first son, Ved Vyas, to father children with Ambika and Ambalika through niyoga in order to continue the royal line.

Q18. Why was Dhritarashtra born blind, and Pandu born frail? A: Per this teaching, Ambika closed her eyes in fear during her union with Vyas, resulting in her son Dhritarashtra being born blind; Ambalika turned pale with fear during her own union, resulting in her son Pandu being born physically frail and pale.

Q19. How was Vidura born, and why couldn't he become king despite being fully capable? A: Per this teaching, when Satyavati requested one more attempt, Ambika sent her maidservant to Vyas in her place out of fear; the maid, approaching without fear , bore a fully capable son, Vidura — but because his mother was a maidservant rather than a queen, he could not inherit the throne.

Q20. Who is Vidura r eally , per this teaching? A: Per this teaching, Vidura is an incarnation of Yamraj, born as the result of a curse: Rishi Mandavya, wrongly executed alongside real thieves despite his innocence, protested Yamraj's justification (a childhood act of killing insects) as disproportionate, and cursed Yamraj to personally experience the pain of injustice and loss as a mortal.

Q21. Does this teaching give a final answer on whether routine pest contr ol (like insecticide spray) carries the same dosh as killing insects in Rishi Mandavya's story? A: Not yet — per this teaching's live practice, Bhaiya indicates the fuller context will become clear once the complete story is heard, without giving a definitive answer in this particular exchange.

Q22. What ar e Prakriti and Sanskriti, per this teaching, and how do they r elate? A: Per this teaching, Prakriti (nature, equated with the whole cosmos and ultimately Adi Shakti) cannot be directly controlled or altered; to draw anything out of pure Prakriti requires first establishing a Sanskriti (a bounded cultural/ener getic framework) built from three elements — an Agni tattva, a Dev tattva, and a Shiv tattva.

Q23. Why can a specific deity be "challenged" by a powerful practitioner , but not Adi Shakti herself? A: Per this teaching, because a specific deity belongs to one particular Sanskriti (culture) and can be made to bow within that framework, whereas Adi Shakti is Prakriti itself — the encompassing nature within which all such cultures exist — and cannot be challenged by anyone.

Q24. Where does Adi Shakti come fr om, per this teaching? A: Per this teaching, Bhagwan Shiva's form as Sada Shiva meditates exclusively on Ram Tattva (described as the supreme param tattva); through this meditation, Shiva manifests the Shakti who sits beside him as Adi Shakti — meaning Prakriti itself is described as ultimately originating from Ram Tattva by way of Shiva.

Q25. Does this teaching encourage making pr edictions about the futur e (such as the Kalki avatar)? A: No — per this teaching, when a sangat member shared predictions they'd heard about the Kalki avatar , Bhaiya declined to engage in prophecy himself, redirecting the focus to studying one's own scriptures rather than speculating about the future.

Q26. Why does this teaching emphasize learning scriptur e and stories acr oss many r eligious traditions, not just Hinduism? A: Per this teaching, both for one's own spiritual growth and so that this knowledge can be passed on to future generations — and because sants engage most meaningfully with seekers who show genuine understanding, not blind devotion alone.
Bot Response Guidelines

Present all mythological/narrative material (Q4–Q20) as "per this teaching," not as settled historical or scriptural fact, and preserve this teaching's own noted textual variants (e.g., the Bengali Mahabharata detail in the Bhishma section) rather than flattening them into a single certain account. For Q21, do not supply a definitive answer about pest control and dosh beyond what this teaching itself states — this question was explicitly left open pending a future session. Keep the mukti/history-repeats-itself teachings (Q1–Q3) framed as encouragement toward present-moment devotion and duty , not as discouraging bhakti or spiritual aspiration. Present the Prakriti/Sanskriti/Adi Shakti cosmology (Q22–Q24) as this teaching's own specific framework, not as a universally agreed Hindu doctrine. Part III — Curated Conversational Q&A (Hinglish)
Bhaiya's Teachings — Curated Conversational Supplement (Session 78, Hinglish)
Mukti Ek Myth Hai, Series Planning, aur Insect-Killing Dosh par ek Live Sawaal

Note: yeh session mostly ek continuous narrated Chandravanshi discourse tha (Mahabhisha, Ganga, Bhishma, Satyavati, Vidura ki kahani), lekin kuch genuine live exchanges bhi the. Sirf wahi exchanges chune gaye hain jo naya sikhate hain ya sabhi users ke kaam aa sakein.
Bhaiya (session shuru hone se pehle, sangat ko wait karte hue): िहतेश भैया बताओ िकतना टाइम और लगेगा? 8:50 तक ठीक है। चलो 7 िमनट और , हम थोड़ा टाइम पास कर लेते हैं, सीताराम कर लेते हैं।

Yeh exchange isliye include kiya gaya kyunki yeh session ka r elaxed, family-jaisa opening dikhata hai — formal teaching shuru hone se pehle bhi kitna comfortable mahaul hai, aur logistics bhi live discuss ho rahe hain.
Sangat (Bhaiya se poochte hue): भैया, ये जो िहस्ट�ी िरपीट हो रही है, तो अभी कलयुग में ना हो िरपीट, उसका कोई उपाय बताया बाबा ने?

Bhaiya (mukti ke concept ko explain karte hue): देिखए , मैं आपको बता देता हूं। पहले जो लोग ये बोलते हैं िक मुिक्त मुिक्त — मुिक्त एक िमथ है। िजतने भी बड़े िसद्ध महात्मा हुए , आज तक उन्होंने कभी भी भगवान से मुिक्त नहीं मांगी। मात सीता से वरदान लेकर वो भगवान से अनन्य भिक्त मांगते हैं, इसके अलावा कुछ नहीं। मुिक्त िमलने के बाद भी, एक िदन कोई ना कोई आपको देखेगा, आपको प�णाम करेगा, और वहीं से कम� बंधन िफर शुरू। तो मुिक्त का कांसेप्ट ही छोड़ दीिजए।
